name: Nikhil Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ride an electric cargo bike in the old town, where vans can't get through. I'm logged into three apps at once, parcels in the morning and food from about five, and I use an AI assistant on my phone to tell me which orders to stack so I'm not riding empty. On a good day I do forty drops and I'm one of the top earners in the area. The hills on Castle Lane are what wear me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you use an AI assistant. How did that start?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I just tried it one wet Sunday, asked it to look at my earnings by hour and street, and it showed me I was wasting Tuesday mornings. Now I use it every day. I live on my own in a studio above a launderette on Canal Road, so my evenings are me, the bike and a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. AI is a good tool, not a god. I'd post my earnings chart in the riders' forum and say, look, it helps you stack orders, that's all it was ever going to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, it's fine. My money's decent for this job, I've got about four months saved, and I'm already using the tools that do exist. Hype or no hype, a cargo bike still beats a van on Castle Lane every single day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep riding and keep teaching other riders how to use the assistant for stacking, because that's real money for them. I'd also keep pushing the idea some of us have of a rider-owned app, a co-op, which feels more doable if AI isn't changing everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Maybe a little bored, because I like change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd teach other riders. Why give away your edge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the apps already have the edge over all of us. If every rider stacks better, the platform has to pay attention. I run a little session in the café on Mill Street every few weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a rider co-op actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Riders own the app, take a fair cut, and decide rates together. There's one in another city I follow online. With AI tools cheap, building the software isn't the hard part anymore, the trust is.

say: AI is a **good tool, not a god**, and it mostly helps stack orders.
Riders should use the **real tools** that exist instead of fearing hype.
think: His **income and savings** look fine, and he already uses what AI offers.
The **cargo bike** keeps its edge in the narrow old town.
do: Keep riding **three apps** with his AI assistant planning order stacks.
Run **café sessions** teaching other riders to stack orders with AI.
Keep building interest in a **rider-owned co-op** app.
feel: **Calm**, and a little bored by a world without change.
S0.quote: Hype or no hype, a cargo bike still beats a van on Castle Lane every single day.
fieldNote: He shares his **tool knowledge** freely, seeing platforms, not riders, as the competition.
His progressive side shows in the **co-op idea** rather than in protest.
He's one of the **top earners** in his area, which keeps him relaxed.

steps.text: Keep stacking orders on three apps with his AI assistant
Run a stacking session for riders at the Mill Street café
Keep riding the old town on the cargo bike

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when riders should organise, not to block AI but to own a piece of it. The apps will use better AI for dispatch and support, so we should use it too. I'd be loud about that online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's mostly good for me. The thinking side of the job is already on my phone, and the bike side is safe for a good while. The apps will get smarter, so the riders who use AI every day will be the ones still earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year getting serious about the co-op: find ten riders, put in two hundred each, and test a simple app with AI handling the customer chat. I'd keep riding full time while we test. If it fails, I lose two hundred pounds and learn a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit nervous for riders who won't touch the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think won't touch the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the older guys, like Marek, who's been riding twenty years and refuses even the map app. He's a better rider than me, but he'll get squeezed when dispatch gets clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put more than two hundred in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe up to five hundred. More than that and I'd be eating into my four months of rent, and I'm not stupid with that money.

say: Riders should **organise to own** a piece of AI, not to block it.
If the apps get **smarter dispatch**, riders need smart tools too.
think: The job's **thinking side** is already on his phone, and the riding is safe for now.
Riders who **use AI daily** will keep earning as apps get smarter.
do: Recruit **ten riders** to put in £200 each for a co-op test.
Test a simple **co-op app** with AI handling the customer chat.
Keep **riding full time** while the co-op is tested.
feel: **Excited** about the chance to build something.
**Nervous** for older riders who avoid new tools.
S1.quote: The apps will get smarter, so the riders who use AI every day will be the ones still earning.
fieldNote: He caps his own risk at **£500**, protecting four months of rent.
He worries for a **veteran colleague** who refuses tools despite being skilled.
Steady Disruption looks like **opportunity** to him because his day is mostly hands-on.

steps.text: Recruit ten riders to put £200 each into a co-op
Test a co-op app with AI answering customer chats
Keep riding full time on three apps during the test

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to belong to everyone, not to three companies. Public ownership of the big AI, or a share of it for everyone. I'd say it online and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel the clock. By 2028 the apps run themselves, and by 2031 there are robots that can carry a parcel up Castle Lane. I've got maybe three years of riding left in that picture, and my whole plan was riding plus a co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch plans in the first months: sign up for a robotics maintenance course, because someone has to fix the delivery robots when they arrive. I'd keep riding to pay for it, and I'd cut my rent by moving into a shared flat to make my savings last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like change, but this is change with no brakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said someone has to fix the robots. Won't AI do that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe eventually. But in the first years they'll need people on the ground with spanners and laptops. I'd rather be one of those than one of the riders watching from the kerb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell first about moving into a shared flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, because she'd worry less if I'm with people. And the guy at the launderette, Hassan, who's basically my landlord's eyes. He'd miss me.

say: AI must **belong to everyone**, through public ownership or a shared stake.
Three companies shouldn't own the **whole future** of work.
think: He'd have about **three years** of riding before robots arrive in 2031.
His **rider-plus-co-op** plan wouldn't survive this speed.
do: Sign up for a **robotics maintenance** course in the first months.
Keep **riding** to pay for the course.
Move into a **shared flat** to stretch his savings.
S2.quote: I've got maybe three years of riding left in that picture, and my whole plan was riding plus a co-op.
fieldNote: Even for someone who **likes change**, two years feels too fast.
He aims to **fix robots** rather than compete with them.
Cutting rent by **sharing a flat** is his main money move.

steps.text: Enrol in a robotics maintenance course this year
Move from the Canal Road studio into a shared flat
Keep riding three apps to pay course fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly. A public stake in AI, training for riders, and co-ops getting a fair shot at the robot fleets. I'd keep saying the riders should own the robots, not just get replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years plus three is a good runway for me. I'd be thirty-five when the robots arrive around 2034. Give me eight years and I'll be the guy running the robot fleet, not the guy it replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the co-op test in year one like in the slower picture. Around year two I'd do the robotics course part-time. By 2031 I'd want the co-op to own a couple of delivery robots, if the price is sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but energised. It's a race I think I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be buying robots that replace riders. How does that sit with your politics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair, and it bugs me. But if riders own them, the money stays with riders. A robot owned by a co-op is better than one owned by a billionaire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots might be too expensive for a small co-op, and the big apps might undercut us. Then I'd fall back on the maintenance work.

say: There's time to give **co-ops** a fair shot at the robot fleets.
Riders should **own the robots**, not just be replaced by them.
think: Eight years until robots is a **good runway** for him.
He sees himself **running a fleet** by his mid-thirties.
do: Start the **co-op test** in the first year.
Take the **robotics course** part-time from year two.
Aim for the co-op to **buy delivery robots** by 2031 if prices allow.
feel: **Uneasy but energised**, as if facing a race he can run.
S3.quote: Give me eight years and I'll be the guy running the robot fleet, not the guy it replaced.
fieldNote: He admits a **tension** between his politics and buying robots that replace riders.
His answer is **ownership**: robots owned by riders keep money with riders.
He has a **fallback** in maintenance work if the co-op fails.

steps.text: Launch the rider co-op test with ten riders
Study robotics maintenance part-time from year two
Save towards the co-op buying two delivery robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and final picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to build something fair. Rider co-ops, public training, a share of AI profits for everyone. This is the picture where we can actually win the argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's great for me. I'd have thirteen years until the robots, and I'd be forty by then, with skills and maybe a business. Ten years is long enough to turn a cargo bike courier into a small business owner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep riding for a couple of years and grow the co-op slowly. I'd use AI every day to run the books and the scheduling. Later I'd learn robotics, so the co-op is ready when robots get cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and hopeful. A bit impatient, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you impatient?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching big firms waste years when we could be building now. I'd want things to move faster than ten years, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does living alone change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes it easier. No kids, no partner to convince, low rent. I can take risks most people my age with families can't.

say: Ten years is enough to build **fair work**: co-ops, training and shared AI profits.
This is the picture where riders can **win the argument**.
think: He'd have **thirteen years** before robots arrive, with skills and maybe a business.
A **cargo bike courier** can become a small business owner in that time.
do: Keep riding while growing the **co-op** slowly over two years.
Use **AI daily** for the co-op's books and scheduling.
Learn **robotics** later so the co-op is ready for cheap robots.
feel: **Calm and hopeful**, and a little impatient.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to turn a cargo bike courier into a small business owner.
fieldNote: Living alone with **low rent** lets him take risks others can't.
He's **impatient** with slow change rather than afraid of it.
His plans stay **consistent** across scenarios; only the timing shifts.

steps.text: Grow the rider co-op slowly while riding part-time
Run the co-op's books and rota with AI tools
Learn robotics before delivery robots get cheap

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I'd starve, but because my plans would break before they start. What would help is cheap evening courses in robotics and public money for co-ops, so riders aren't just shut out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns the robots. Delivery robots are coming either way, and the only question is whether riders own any of them. Nobody asks that.

headlineQuote: Delivery robots are coming either way, and the only question is whether riders own any of them.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old cargo bike courier** in the old town, logged into three apps at once.
He uses an **AI assistant daily** to stack orders and is one of the top earners in his area.
He lives alone above a launderette, with about **four months saved** and low costs.
His big idea is a **rider-owned co-op**, later owning its own delivery robots.
He stays **calm** in slow pictures and becomes **anxious** only when AGI arrives in 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his co-op and riding plans would break before they began.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **evening robotics courses** and **public money** for rider co-ops.
